newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto sacked as prime minister for second time.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto sacked as prime minister for second time.

text.p: Benazir Bhutto, Pakistan's first woman prime minister, was sacked on Tuesday by presidential order for the second time in her roller-coaster political life.
President Farooq Leghari dissolved the National Assembly (lower house) and dismissed Bhutto, 43, citing corruption and other abuses of power by her three-year-old government.
He named Meraj Khalid, 80, as interim prime minister to supervise elections to be held on February 3, 1997.
Bhutto has twice tasted power in a career that has seen her in the country's jails as well as its corridors of power.
She had previously sworn to ride out the political and economic storms battering her government and seek a fresh mandate at elections she said would be held in October 1998.
She portrayed herself abroad as a woman struggling against the odds to steer her turbulent Islamic country on a moderate course of economic liberalisation and social justice.
But Leghari's proclamation of her dismissal contained a sweeping, detailed indictment of her administration.
The president said her government had failed to stop extrajudicial killings in Karachi, allowed extensive corruption and nepotism, and sought to undermine the judiciary.

Leghari accused Bhutto, his former political ally, of insinuating that the presidency and other state agencies were involved in a conspiracy to kill her brother Murtaza Bhutto, shot dead in Karachi on September 20 with seven companions.
Other critics have flayed her for leading what they say is a corrupt, inept government that has fumbled its foreign policy, flirted with economic ruin and trampled on human rights.
There has been harsh media criticism of her husband Asif Ali Zardari, who became Investment Minister in July. He has denied accusations of corruption and influence-peddling.
"We are into our Golden Jubilee celebrations and several visits of foreign dignitaries, including the Queen (Elizabeth), are scheduled ahead," Bhutto told reporters on Sunday.
"I don't think any patriotic Pakistani would therefore wish to see the government dissolved," she declared.

A European diplomat said on Monday that evoking Pakistan's 50th anniversary, not to mention a royal visit 12 months away, as a reason for her foes to ease up smacked of desperation. "But she is a fighter who is not going to give up easily," he said.
The diplomat said the prime minister, not reputed to be a good listener, may have become insulated from reality during three years in power, but was now belatedly aware of her danger.
Bhutto's troubles have proliferated in the past two months.
Leghari had taken a higher profile since September, seeking a greater role in appointing top judges, demanding that parliament combat corruption and meeting opposition leaders.

Lawyers for Ghinwa Bhutto, Murtaza's widow, accused Zardari, Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar and Sindh Province Chief Minister Abdullah Shah last month of conspiring to kill the prime minister's brother. They deny the charge.

Last month a strike called by the main opposition party led by Nawaz Sharif was followed by anti-corruption protests by the religious Jamaat-i-Islami party that police in Islamabad and nearby Rawalpindi quelled with teargas and batons.
On Sunday the Lahore High Court reinstated Manzoor Wattoo as chief minister of Punjab province on Sunday, saying his ouster last year, on Bhutto's recommendation, had been unlawful.
Pakistan's dire financial woes forced the government to devalue the rupee and impose a tough new budgetary package last month to avert a possible foreign currency crisis.

Bhutto, who had held the finance portfolio herself for three years, finally gave it up this month, naming Naveed Qamar as finance minister to head a revamped economic team and negotiate a new agreement with the International Monetary Fund.
Bhutto clawed her way back to recapture the post of prime minister in the October 1993 parliamentary election after three years in the political wilderness.

Bhutto launched into politics after army chief General Mohammed Zia-ul-Haq overthrew her father, Pakistan's first popularly elected leader Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, in July 1977 and then hanged him in 1979 on a controversial murder conviction.

She inherited leadership of the Pakistan's People's Party (PPP) after her father's execution in 1979, fighting vainly against Zia for 11 years. Bhutto and her mother Nusrat were often in prison or under house arrest.
In August 1988 Zia died in a mystery air crash. Bhutto, weak from the birth of her first son, took to the hustings and the magic of the Bhutto name proved as potent as ever.
She won 39 percent of the vote and her PPP became the biggest party in parliament, but short of an overall majority.
Her election victory was welcomed worldwide as the advent of democracy in Pakistan after more than a decade of military rule, but the establishment banded against her.

Bhutto, a mother of three and an inveterate traveller, impressed foreign audiences, but economic and security problems -- notably a long-running conflict with the ethnic Mohajir National Movement in Karachi -- dented her popularity at home.

She gave short shrift to political foes, pursuing corruption cases against former prime minister Nawaz Sharif and his family in the courts and virtually banning coverage in the state media of cricketer-turned-politician Imran Khan.
President Ghulam Ishaq Khan sacked her after just 20 months, accusing her of presiding over large-scale corruption.
Bhutto, who always appears with an Islamic-style scarf on her head, was born on June 21, 1953 in Karachi, the first of four children. Benazir means "unique".
She was educated at a Christian mission school in Karachi, Radcliffe (now part of Harvard) University, and Britain, where she became president of the Oxford Union debating society.
